newsitem.title: UK: Era seen ending as current UK parliament winds up.
newsitem.headline: Era seen ending as current UK parliament winds up.

text.p: If the opinion polls are right, Friday marked the beginning of the end of a political era in Britain.
But, whatever the impact of the social and economic revolution carried out in 18 years of unbroken Conservative rule, the age-old traditions of the nation's parliament remain undisturbed.

While Prime Minister John Major and opposition Labour leader Tony Blair traded allegations of sleaze and smear on the campaign trail, bewigged peers in fur-lined robes expressed Queen Elizabeth's desire to close parliament to allow a general election to be held on May 1.
The arcane ritual held a special poignancy for the 90 or so members of parliament retiring after the May 1 election.
Many of these turned up to follow the quaintly titled official, Black Rod, from the House of Commons to the House of Lords to hear the royal proclamation.

But hundreds of Conservatives members of the lower house who stayed away from the ceremony are also affected by emotion -- fear that voters may decide they too should not return to the neo-Gothic splendour of the Palace of Westminster, seat of Britain's parliament.

Polls give the opposition Labour party a lead of 25 percentage points or more, a margin no sitting government has ever overcome in the official campaign -- in this case one lasting six weeks. Voters seem to be ready for a change.

Major, who has overseen an economic boom with falling unemployment, low inflation and rising prosperity, may be wryly reflecting on the words some blame for the fall of the last Labour government in 1979: "Crisis. What crisis?"
The phrase, ascribed to Labour's last prime minister, Jim Callaghan, by The Sun newspaper -- and denied by Callaghan -- gave an impression of a government out of touch with voters.
Polls show Major is tarred with the same brush. He continues to claim that only victory lies ahead for the Conservatives.

In 1979, the Labour government was blamed for a "winter of discontent" during which car workers, ambulancemen, water and sewerage workers, and local authority staff went on strike to protest at the government's efforts to restrain wages.
Callaghan, in charge of a minority government whose party structure was in disarray, finally fell after his plans for devolution of power to Scotland and Wales collapsed.
Conservative leader Margaret Thatcher swept to power in an election which showed the strength of a disciplined national party organisation and a slick advertising campaign.

Thatcher ripped into the unions, curbing their power, launched a wave of privatisations and brought market forces to bear on almost every aspect of voters' lives -- from health to education, water supplies to public transport.

Major was installed by the Conservatives in 1990 as concern over Thatcher's autocratic style boiled over. He was the calm after the storm and won the 1992 election almost single-handed with a reduced majority of 21 in the 651-seat House of Commons.

But Major's inability to heal his party's divisions over future relations within the European Union eclipsed his achievement of taming inflation after inheriting Britain's worst recession since World War Two.
His anger at the unfairness of it all burst forth in the final confrontation with Blair in this parliament on Thursday, the day before the formal ceremony to end proceedings.
Shouting across the chamber, he accused Blair of having "traded in double standards from the moment you took office".
It was a far cry from the measured tones and respectful ceremony of Friday and smacked of desperation.
If the pundits are right, when parliament returns it will be filled by a new generation of MPs, many of them newcomers and the majority of them Labour. But the ceremonies will be the same.
